_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Nieman Storyboard] Personal stories of 9/11, 25 years later
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Sign up for the Nieman Storyboard newsletter, delivered every Friday in your inbox.

***

Dear Storyboard community:

I moved from California to New York City in late August 2001. 

I had been living in Manhattan for two weeks when I showed up for work in Times Square and discovered that a plane had struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center, just a few miles south. 

After the second plane struck the South Tower at 9:03 am ET, our office building was evacuated. I gathered my belongings, walked east to Fifth Avenue, and slowly made my way uptown, turning around every couple blocks to see the massive plumes of smoke in the distance. 

By the time I reached Central Park, crowds gathered around televisions outside the CBS News studios on 59th Street. I remember the looks on people's faces, in tears, in shock, as they replayed footage of the South Tower collapsing. 

In the days that followed, I spent many nights in Union Square, on 14th Street. It had become a gathering place for candlelight vigils and collective grieving. Posters for missing friends and family members were taped up everywhere. 

I felt fortunate to be a part of this community as it came together, to be a witness to it. But for many years I felt like this was not my story to tell. I lost no friends or family members. I was barely even a New Yorker. What right did I have to share my experience? 

And yet, as I've gotten older I've come to appreciate the importance of telling my own stories. My daughters have interviewed me about 9/11 for school reports. As Garrett Graff writes for National Geographic, “Today some 40 percent of the country is too young to remember the events of 9/11.” Every story, however small, adds to our collective memory and shared understanding. They connect us. 

I think frequently about the power of "Portraits of Grief,” the New York Times project in which reporters crafted 200-word vignettes for 2,310 of the nearly 3,000 people who died on 9/11. “We weren't mourning an anonymous mass of people, we were mourning thousands of individuals,” the late novelist Paul Auster wrote about the profiles in 2001. “And the more we knew about them, the more we could wrestle with our own grief.”

For more stories and remembrances from 9/11, see the Nieman Storyboard archive.

You have your own story to share, too. My guest on this week's Nieman Storyboard podcast, author and editor Sari Botton, taught me so much about the power of personal storytelling when she was the essays editor for Longreads. She's now editor and publisher of popular Substack publications including Oldster Magazine and Memoir Land, and she's written her own memoir, “And You May Find Yourself…Confessions of a Late-Blooming Gen-X Weirdo.” She shares some important insights about her journey, as well as advice for writers who might be working on their own personal stories.

Author and editor Sari Botton on giving yourself permission to write personal essays

“People are so concerned about whether they're going to be a likable character if they tell the ugly truth. [But] that's what makes you a likable character. It makes you someone that people can relate to. It means you're just human.”

[ Read the story ]


[ Follow us in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. ]

Links of note

  • “Don’t Make My Mistakes: A Guide to Reporting in Unfamiliar Places.” For Study Hall, journalist Hannah Docter-Loeb breaks down the key questions reporters should consider when writing about a community that is new to them. 

  • Science journalist Christian Elliott explains how one of his sources for a National Geographic story, a 77-year-old retired librarian named Phil Gordon, was so interesting that he became the main character in an entirely different profile. “I spent maybe two hours with Gordon in total,” Elliott writes. “In that time, he dropped so many quotable lines I had more material than I knew what to do with. When we drove up (and parked behind his dented white pickup, full of driftwood logs collected on the beach for unspecified reasons), [we] found him sitting on a rickety wooden platform dangling over Pacific Ocean. He offered us bourbon and peanut butter.”

  • Journalist Leah Sottile reflects on six years of writing her newsletter (and perhaps another data point in whether you should start your own): “It has since become a major part of my writing life — a thing I very much look forward to working on each month. So, yeah, I guess it made me feel better. Sometimes the writing comes to me easily, sometimes I totally panic about writing something worthy of your hard-earned dollars. It has never been my goal to be the biggest writer on Substack, and it shocks me every time I meet someone in the real world who says they are one of the 5,132 people reading this newsletter every month. There is something that just punches me in the heart every time I hear that, makes me feel so seen, like I’m not just out here making my hands arthritic for no good reason.” 

Keep writing and sharing your stories,

Mark Armstrong
Editor
Nieman Storyboard
Follow the Nieman Storyboard Podcast 
On Bluesky: @niemanstoryboard.org

items.title: [Fast Company] Maersk is testing a giant spinning cylinder to cut fuel use on cargo ships
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

On a cargo ship packed with 8,700 shipping containers, there isn’t much room for anything else. But in a new test aboard one of its vessels, Maersk is making an exception for a giant rotor sail—a spinning cylinder 10 to 12 stories tall that harnesses wind to help reduce fuel use.

The test comes as shipping fuel costs continue to soar. In some areas, the price has risen as much as 76% since the Iran war started. The tech, made by a U.K.-based company called Anemoi, is one way to help blunt future price spikes while also cutting carbon emissions for one of the world’s most polluting industries. It’s also an example of how the industry is increasingly making use of wind power.

The 115-foot-tall rotor sail works much like an aircraft wing, which generates lift as air moves faster over the top of a wing than underneath.

“Our rotor sails work on the same basic principle of creating a pressure difference, but instead of a wing, we use a tall spinning cylinder,” says Anemoi CEO Clare Urmston. “As the cylinder spins, it speeds the airflow on one side and slows it down on the other. This creates low pressure on one side and high pressure on the other, producing the force that pushes the ship forward.”

In some cases, each sail can reduce around 1 ton of fuel use per day, but depending on wind conditions, that can jump to as much as a 20-ton reduction. Each ton of fuel saved also saves the equivalent of 3 tons of CO2 emissions. It’s not turning a cargo ship into a sailing vessel—a ship like Maersk’s can use 100 tons of fuel in a day. (Some other companies, like Vela, are building cargo ships that do run entirely or almost entirely on wind.)

But the fuel savings are significant, and could translate into saving hundreds of thousands of dollars for a vessel in a year. The payback period for one of the devices is typically five years, but it can be faster for ships operating in Europe under stricter regulations for shipping emissions.

In the past, Anemoi has worked with other types of vessels, like bulk carriers transporting raw materials. But the new installation with Maersk is its first on a container ship. In theory, the wind flow around the shipping containers may actually help the sail perform better.

“It’s the first of its type,” Urmston says. “So we’re really excited to be part of this pioneering study and see how that works. It could be a big change for the container ship market going forward if successful.”

The rotor sail will be installed on the Maersk ship in mid-2027; the company will then track performance as the ship goes on a regular route across the Atlantic. Though the vessel uses standard shipping fuel now, the technology could also help as ships transition to lower-carbon fuels in the future.

“Wind is really attractive because it doesn’t require predicting which fuel will be burnt in the future, so it’s complementary to all alternative fuels,” Urmston says. Because alternative fuels are more expensive right now, she adds, there’s even more of a case for adding wind to help.

items.title: [Fast Company] 25 years after 9/11, some parts of air travel are starting to look familiar again. Here’s how much flying has changed
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

It’s hard to believe that 9/11 was 25 years ago today. On that day, September 11, 2001, I was a young journalist working at CNN headquarters, producing the noon newscast, when I saw the first, and then the second, plane crash into the World Trade Center in real time on the newsroom monitor.

In an instant, everything about air travel in America changed. And 9/11 has informed the way we have traveled ever since. Gone are the days when anybody could say goodbye to loved ones at the gate. (Although that restriction has recently begun to ease; more on that below.) Also gone, for the most part: the ability to run late and still make your flight in under half an hour.

Here are a few examples of what is different between then and now.

TSA airport security checks

While there were security checks before September 11, 2001, they were nothing in comparison to the invasive TSA screening checkpoints we have today. Those screenings are a direct result of the formation of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), which was created in November 2001, two months after the terrorist attacks.

Back then, there were no required Real IDs, no full-body screenings or mandatory metal detectors with enhanced screening technology, no need to show your ID before security, and certainly no invasive privacy measures such as facial scans employing facial recognition software.

Beyond just taking off our shoes or having to scan the contents of our carry-ons, those of us who remember long for the days when we could show up late to the gate, drink in hand, and board with relative ease.

Originally, the TSA was housed under the Department of Transportation (DOT), whose focus under the Aviation and Transportation Security Act (signed by then-President George Bush two months after the attacks) was to perform uniform, restrictive screening, and institute a federal takeover of airport security from private companies.

But in 2003, the agency moved to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Starting in 2011 with the launch of TSA PreCheck, TSA created a system that critics now argue over-screens the general public, treating every passenger as a threat instead of focusing on high-risk individuals. From body scans that employ advanced imaging technologies to restricting liquids, aerosols, and gels, airport security measures have made traveling a long, exhausting process. TSA screened 900 million people at airports in just 2025 alone.

In fact, today’s TSA’s Secure Flight program’s security measures “begin long before you arrive at the airport.” Most travelers are probably unaware that TSA screens passenger information, cross-listing it with intelligence and federal government watch lists—for both travel outside the U.S. but also within—before you even hit security.

Boarding passes

A boarding pass is now required to get to the gate. It wasn’t always. After the September 11 attacks, printed boarding passes became mandatory requirements to pass through security. By 2010, mobile boarding passes accessible from smartphones became standard.

However, this post-9/11 restriction is now starting to ease. In a welcome change for many, TSA is instituting TSA Gateside, which will ease restrictions on those who want to see off friends and family at the gate. As Fast Company previously reported, PreCheck members at select airports can now go to the gates to meet flights, even if they aren’t flying themselves.

Longer lines, even at TSA PreCheck

Since 9/11, airport wait times have occasionally averaged one to three hours at certain hubs, per NPR.

And according to a 2025 New York Times article, TSA PreCheck, which was created to cut down on the long lines formed by post-9/11 security checkpoints, doesn’t actually speed up travel by much. Reporters looked into travel at New York airports, and found PreCheck at John F. Kennedy, LaGuardia, and Newark airports only saved travelers about five to 10 minutes on average.

What travel restrictions have eased since 9/11?

Passengers have welcomed the end of the shoe removal rule, which, while not a direct result of 9/11, was also instituted around the same time.

Also expediting the security process: Some busy mothers now can access new dedicated lanes for families, as can veterans, at select airports.

items.title: [Fast Company] It took 2,977 drones to create this stunning 9/11 memorial show. Here’s how they pulled it off
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

To remember the lives of the 2,977 people killed in the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago, 2,977 drones were arranged in the shape of the original Minoru Yamasaki-designed World Trade Center at full architectural scale for a stunning temporary memorial. It took a lot of planning to make it work.

Called “2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor,” the commemorative public art installation on September 9 was sponsored by the New York Foundation for the Arts, and pulling it off required coordination with dozens of agencies. One of the biggest challenges was finding a suitable launch location.

“We need a lot of space to set the drones down,” Kyle Pivnick, vice president of Texas-based Sky Elements Drones, tells Fast Company, noting that thousands of hours went into finding the right path to bring the memorial to life.

The installation was produced by Sky Elements (which has put on professional drone shows for Formula 1 and Lollapalooza) in partnership with creative director Addison Mehr, Studio Drift, Ideko, designer Yan Paul Dubbelman, and artistic advisers Shigeru Ban and Dean Maltz, with input from 9/11 families, survivors, and first responders.

The installation’s creators needed about 12,000 square feet of flat, open-sky ground, which isn’t easy to find in New York City. Eventually, the U.S. Coast Guard agreed to let the creators use a parking lot at its recruitment office on the southern tip of Manhattan as the staging area.

The show was held for just one night, and it required flight restrictions so there would be no air traffic in the area, as well securing the ground below from people and moving vehicles, which is why it was held over the waterfront instead of the original World Trade Center location.

Using exactly 2,977 drones, one for each life lost at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and the United Airlines crash site in Pennsylvania on September 11, 2001, was foundational to the project. But that meant being deliberate about where to fill and add detail when re-creating the Twin Towers, Pivnick says.

“More drones would of course be better to give the towers more detail, but the choice to keep the drone count at 2,977 was paramount,” he says.

Drone shows are popular for advertising or entertainment events, but for “2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor,” the goal was to create an experience that was reverent and respectful.

The drones first appeared like two upward-swirling helixes before slowly rearranging into the shape of the towers. The helix shape was meant to recall the unbuilt proposal for a World Cultural Center memorial designed by Think that featured two open latticework towers.

By re-creating the towers as tall as they once stood, the installation gave a sense of scale and a feeling that’s larger than life. By using exactly 2,977 drones, the remembrance was poignant and personal.
